report:
### Conclusion
Scientific evidence strongly supports the claim that consuming higher amounts of olive oil reduces the risk of stroke.

### Supporting Evidence
Multiple meta-analyses and prospective cohort studies report a significant inverse relationship between olive oil intake and stroke risk. A comprehensive meta-analysis found that consuming approximately two tablespoons (25g) of olive oil daily was associated with a 26% lower stroke risk (https://www.myolivea.com/blogs/research/olive-oil-stroke-cardiovascular-meta-analysis-2014). Dose-response evaluations similarly indicate optimal protective effects at daily intakes between 20 and 30 grams (https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614(21)00503-3/pdf).

Strong clinical evidence comes from the PREDIMED randomized controlled trial, where a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil reduced major cardiovascular events, including stroke, by about 30% compared to a low-fat control diet (https://healthcrunch.org/articles/2026-02-26-mediterranean-diet-stroke-risk-women-study). Biological mechanisms include olive oil's high concentration of monounsaturated fatty acids (oleic acid) and antioxidant polyphenols, which lower blood pressure, reduce vascular inflammation, and improve lipid profiles.

### Limitations & Counter-Evidence
Despite consistent findings, observational research carries limitations:
* **Confounding Factors:** High olive oil intake frequently co-occurs with healthier overall lifestyles, higher socioeconomic status, and diets rich in vegetables and seafood, making it challenging to isolate olive oil's effect entirely.
* **Dietary Context:** Meta-analyses show that overall adherence to a Mediterranean diet yields a pooled stroke risk reduction (HR 0.88) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39777701/), suggesting olive oil provides maximum benefit when combined with an overall healthy eating pattern rather than consumed in isolation.
